items.title: Model-API credential proxy: agent gets a placeholder, a sidecar injects the real token (#121 phase 1, injection point A2)
items.body:
Phase 1 of #121, taking injection point **A2** (proxy injects) rather than A1 (broker hands a token to the agent).

`THREAT_MODEL.md` accepts R3 (exfiltration via allowed hosts) and today mitigates it only partially, via `SANDY_SUSPICIOUS=1` refresh-token stripping. Claude Code's own docs describe the same pattern for cloud sessions: *"a separate proxy holds your GitHub token outside the sandbox while issuing scoped credentials for repository access inside it."*

## Proposal

Do the model API first, since it is the one credential **every** sandy session carries.

- A credential sidecar on the internal network holds the real credential. Started by the host launcher per session (or per project), removed on exit.
- The agent container gets the sidecar's address as its API base URL and a **fixed placeholder** in the credential variable. No real token is mounted or exported into the box.
- The sidecar strips any auth headers the agent sent, adds the real credential, forwards only to the configured model host and only model-API paths, and writes one log line per request (method, path, status, bytes), saved with the session.
- Everything else the agent sends still goes to the existing egress proxy.

## Why it is worth the moving part

- Closes R3 **for the model credential**: a fully compromised box holds a placeholder.
- Under `SANDY_EGRESS_STRICT=1` the model host no longer needs to be agent-reachable at all — only the sidecar needs it.
- `SANDY_SUSPICIOUS` refresh-token stripping becomes unnecessary for this credential.

## To settle during the spike

- **Which variable carries the placeholder.** Claude Code picks its auth header format from *which* env var holds the credential (API key vs OAuth token), and sandy already enforces a one-credential rule with a documented precedence. The placeholder has to live in the variable that actually wins, or the agent will pick a different header shape than the sidecar expects.
- **Proxy-variable interaction.** A plain-http base URL inside the box versus whatever `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY`/`NO_PROXY` sandy sets for the egress proxy.
- **Third-party providers** (Bedrock, Vertex) need request signing or token minting in the sidecar — phase 2, not this.

## Acceptance

- `env` inside a running sandbox shows no real credential in any variable, and no credential file is mounted.
- Model calls succeed and appear in the sidecar log.
- Strict egress with the model host removed from the **agent-reachable** allowlist still completes a session.

Related: #246 (the gh-account slice of the same problem), #244 (a model-API-only allowlist, which this makes more useful).

items.title: RFC: workload-anchored credential binding and layered credential derivation

labels.name: security
labels.description: Cedar/HITL, IAM least-privilege, secrets, PII/DLP, guardrails, supply-chain/CVE

items.body:
**Context:** ROADMAP.md → Workload-anchored credential binding + Layered credential derivation
**Related:** #249, #209, #428, #427

---

## Primary area

Cross-cutting / multiple

## Related issue or feature request

#249 (Identity propagation / Token Vault), #209 (per-session IAM scoping), #428 (runtime security telemetry)

## Summary

Extend ABCA's credential model beyond per-session IAM tags with (1) **workload-anchored binding**—credentials usable only inside the attested MicroVM/workload—and (2) **layered derivation**—progressively narrower tokens at orchestrator → agent runtime → per-tool-call boundaries.

## Use case and motivation

Per-session scoping limits *what* a stolen credential can access but not *where* it can be exercised. A credential exfiltrated from the VM remains valid until expiry. Layered derivation limits blast radius at every hop: orchestrator task token → agent tool-scoped token → single-use external API token.

## Proposal

### Workload-anchored binding

- Bind issued credentials to platform attestation (instance identity document, AgentCore workload identity, or equivalent).
- Token Vault / STS AssumeRole policies reject calls not originating from the bound workload.
- Document operator requirements and failure modes when attestation is unavailable (ECS vs AgentCore).

### Layered derivation

- Orchestrator holds task-scoped delegation token.
- Agent runtime derives further-restricted credentials limited to resolved tools/repos for the current turn.
- External tool invocations receive time-boxed or single-use tokens where the upstream API supports it.
- Propagate signed actor chain (`user_id → orchestrator → agent`) per delegation chain roadmap intent; align with #427.

### Operator / developer experience

- Before: one SessionRole assumption per task; broad tool surface within tag scope.
- After: credentials are non-transferable and monotonically narrower down the stack; audit trail shows full lineage.

## Out of scope

- Replacing Cognito user authentication.
- Full GitHub App implementation (#50)—this RFC defines the credential pattern those integrations consume.
- Bedrock cost attribution (#215)—orthogonal but should share session tags.

## Potential challenges

- Not all external APIs support fine-grained derived tokens.
- Role chaining 1-hour cap vs 8-hour tasks—refresh semantics must be specified.
- Attestation availability differs across AgentCore vs ECS (#164).
- Increased latency on credential mint per tool call.

## Dependencies and integrations

- AgentCore Identity Token Vault (#249 Phase 0 spike).
- `aws_session.py`, orchestrator durable functions, Gateway tool mediation.
- Cedar policies may need new actions for elevation (#422).

## Alternative solutions

- Rely solely on per-session IAM tags (#209)—simpler but does not prevent exfiltration reuse.
- Network-only containment (DNS firewall)—complements but does not replace credential binding.

---

**Note:** Non-triaged RFCs may not get timely review.

items.title: Design: agent sandboxes on spore.host (spawn sandbox, MCP sandbox tools, Managed Agents worker, hypha)

milestone.title: Later
milestone.description: Epics, designs and features not yet scheduled.

items.body:
Design proposal: how spore.host could offer **agent sandboxes** (the category Docker Sandboxes, E2B, Daytona, Modal, Lambda MicroVMs and others sell), and do better for its own audience: GPUs, large memory, data in the user's own AWS account, and hard TTL and cost guarantees. The full research brief is in the first comment. It covers a landscape of about 20 products with sources, a capability map against spawn, design options A–D, phases and experiments. Each claim is tagged [P] primary docs, [3P] third party, [code], EST (estimate) or UNVERIFIED. ## TL;DR 1. **What the market sells.** Nearly every "agent sandbox" is the same thing: a Firecracker microVM, a gVisor container, or a full VM, behind a create/exec/files/snapshot/destroy API. - They start in well under a second to a few seconds, because they restore from snapshots or use warm pools. - They bill per second. - They cap lifetime: 45 min to 24 h on most, 8 h on AWS's two offerings. - They run on the vendor's cloud. - Almost none offer GPUs. Modal and Daytona do. Northflank also claims GPU support [3P]. 2. **The ground shifted in 2026, in two ways.** - **AWS Lambda MicroVMs** went GA on 2026-06-22 [P]. They are Firecracker sandboxes that run **in the customer's own AWS account**, with suspend/resume. Limits: 8 h hard cap, ARM64 only, 16 vCPU / 32 GB at most, and no GPU mentioned. - **EC2 nested virtualization** on C8i/M8i/R8i and some 7th-gen Intel types (announced 2026-02) [P]. Firecracker now runs on ordinary, cheap EC2 instances instead of `.metal`. - Together these remove "your own AWS account" as a unique differentiator for small CPU sandboxes. AWS now sells exactly that. 3. **Claude Managed Agents has a self-hosted sandbox mode** (beta) [P]. A worker inside your infrastructure polls a work queue over outbound HTTPS and runs the agent's tool calls locally. It is already listed with 11 platform guides: Lambda MicroVMs, E2B, Daytona, Modal, Cloudflare, Fly, GKE, Vercel, and others. - The model is almost exactly `spawn pool`: workers in your account pull work from a queue. - This is the cheapest high-leverage integration available to spore.host. 4. **spore.host already has most of a "heavy sandbox"** [code]: - ephemeral EC2 with TTL, cost limit and idle stop, enforced in-instance by a signed `spored`, plus an out-of-band reaper; - truffle sizing, including GPUs, Spot and capacity blocks; - keyless SSM connect; - TaskSpec container runs with `--gpus all`; - SQS worker pools; - S3, EFS and FSx data in the user's account; - an MCP server that can already launch billable tasks behind a mandatory TTL. What it lacks is a **programmatic interactive surface**: exec, file put/get, snapshot/fork, an egress policy, and fast start. Today a sandbox is either a batch task or an SSH session. 5. **Recommendation.** Don't start by building a Firecracker fleet. Build `spawn sandbox`, an agent-facing create/exec/cp/snapshot/destroy surface over EC2 spores (Option A), and expose it through spore-host-mcp (Option C). Ship a **Claude Managed Agents self-hosted worker recipe** on top (Option D1). - Position it as **the sandbox tier incumbents don't serve**: GPUs, big memory, long lifetimes, data in your account, and hard cost/TTL guarantees. - Treat the sub-second tier as a **pluggable backend**: - evaluate Lambda MicroVMs first (buy); - build a nested-virt Firecracker broker (Option B, working name **`hypha`**) only if measurements show it pays off. - Run the de-risking experiments in Part 4 before committing to B. ### 4.2 Phases | Phase | Deliverable | Size | |---|---|---| | **P0: de-risk and decide** (1–2 wks) | Run experiments E1–E3 below. Decide the open questions in 4.4. | S | | **P1: MVP, `spawn sandbox` (Option A1)** | 1. `create / exec / cp / status / extend / destroy`, with exec via SSM and cp via an S3 relay.
2. Egress `none|s3|open` (per-sandbox SG + VPC endpoints).
3. Mandatory TTL **and** cost limit.
4. Reaper-armed precondition.
5. `pkg/sandbox` Go API and Python SDK methods.
6. MCP tools (Option C). | M | | **P1.5: Managed Agents recipe (D1)** | Poller spore plus a per-session sandbox script. Documented and validated on a GPU sandbox reading S3 data. Offer it to Anthropic's platform-guide list. | S | | **P2: v1, fast-enough and forkable** | 1. Pre-baked sandbox AMI (Docker + NVIDIA toolkit + exec agent).
2. Warm/stopped pool claim.
3. `snapshot` / `fork` via AMI.
4. `allow:` egress through the per-account proxy spore.
5. Credential placeholder injection.
6. `--backend lambda-microvm` (Option B′) with reaper coverage for MicroVMs, images and snapshots. | M–L | | **P3: optional, `hypha` (Option B)** | Only if E2 and E3 show:
• Lambda MicroVMs is inadequate (x86, >8 h, FSx mounts, egress, fork, cost at density); **and**
• nested-virt Firecracker hits target latency and density. | L | ### 4.3 First concrete milestone > **`spawn sandbox` A1 + MCP**: > 1. An agent in Claude Code calls `sandbox_create {gpu:1, ttl:"2h", cost_limit:5, egress:"s3", data:["s3://…:ro"]}`. > 2. It runs `nvidia-smi` and a Python script over the mounted dataset via `sandbox_exec`. > 3. It pulls a result file with `sandbox_read_file`, then calls `sandbox_destroy`. > > **Pass criteria:** > - the agent never held AWS keys beyond the local MCP chain; > - the sandbox had no inbound ports and no internet egress; > - the reaper was armed; > - an independent post-run sweep finds zero leaked instances, volumes, SGs, ENIs or instance profiles, and no S3 objects outside the results prefix. ### 4.4 Open questions for the owner 1. **Tenancy.** Sandboxes stay strictly single-account and BYO? Recommendation: yes. A hosted multi-tenant sandbox service would break "data never leaves your account". Any hosted helper must respect the existing cross-account trust constraints: no trusts toward management or internal accounts. 2. **Reaper as a precondition.** Should `sandbox create` hard-require an armed reaper in the target account, or warn plus `--accept-no-backstop`? 3. **MCP spending policy.** The boundary already moved with `spawn_task_run`. Is autonomous sandbox creation acceptable with a mandatory TTL and cost limit plus per-day caps in config? Should GPU sandboxes require an explicit config opt-in? 4. **Egress default.** `none`, `s3`, or `open`? Recommendation: `s3` for data science, with `open` requiring a flag. 5. **Lambda MicroVMs as a backend.** Acceptable to depend on it (ARM64-only, 5 regions, 8 h)? It needs reaper extensions for non-EC2 artifacts. 6. **Managed Agents beta.** Is it acceptable to build a recipe on a beta API (`managed-agents-2026-04-01`)? It is low-cost, because it's a doc plus a script, not core code. 7. **Naming.** Is `hypha` OK for the microVM tier, with `sclerotium` for snapshots and `conidia` for forks? Or should everything live under `spawn sandbox`? 8. **Scope of "fork".** Is a disk-only fork (AMI) enough for v1, or is memory-state fork a requirement? Memory-state fork effectively forces Option B. ## Status - **E1** (EC2 time-to-first-exec) is being run now. Its results will be posted here. - **E2–E4** are specified in the brief, not yet run.
